1.note: The word translated as **saying** introduces a direct quotation. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language.

2.note: This expression uses the possessive form to describe **holy things** (sacrificial food offerings) that the **sons of Israel** offer to Yahweh as sacrifices. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a generic expression. Alternate translation: [the holy things that the sons of Israel offer to Yahweh]
See how you handled this metaphor for the people of Israel in 1:2.

Here, the word **name** represents Yahweh’s reputation and, by extension, Yahweh himself. So to **profane** this **name** is to associate Yahweh who is holy with that which is not only not holy, but abominable and detestable, like child sacrifice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this expression in 20:3. Alternate translation: [and they shall not publicly defame me] or [and they shall not openly denigrate my reputation]

This expression uses the possessive form to describe Yahweh’s **name** (his reputation as God) that is characterized by **holiness**. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a generic expression. Alternate translation: [my holy name] or [my sacred reputation]

3.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell them that to their generations]

Here, the word **your** is plural and refers to the Israelite priests, the male descendants of Aaron. If you chose to make this verse indirect speech (as the previous note suggested), it may be helpful to change the second-person pronouns to the third person. Alternate translation: [to their generations … from all their seed]
Here the word **man** refers to any male descendant of Aaron who serves as a priest. If it would be helpful in your language, consider making this explicit. Alternate translation: [any priest]

This expression uses the word **seed** to refer to one’s children. Whether semen was thought of to resemble plant seed is unclear, although the same word is used to refer to both (see 11:37 and 15:16 for reference). If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this metaphor in 20:2. Alternate translation: [from all your children] or [from all your descendants]

Here a verb and its object come from the same root. The phrase **have made holy** translates a verb that is related to the noun translated as **holy things**. The repetition of related words adds emphasis to the statement. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing emphasis. Alternate translation: [to the holy things that the sons of Israel are presenting to Yahweh as holy offerings]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uncleanness**, you could express the same idea in another way. It may be helpful to see how you translated this abstract noun in 5:3. Alternate translation: [while he is unclean] or [and he is unclean]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:20.

Here, **face** represents the presence of a person. In this expression, the priest who offers sacrifices while he is unclean must be removed from Yahweh’s presence—that is, he must be exiled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from my presence] or [from the place where I live among the Israelites]

4.note: Here the word **man** refers to any priest. See how you handled the repetition of the word **man** in 15:2. Alternate translation: [Any priest]
See how you handled this metaphor for descendants in 20:2. Alternate translation: [from the children of Aaron] or [from Aaron’s descendants]

The terms **skin diseased** and **flowing** refer to various kinds of visible, infectious skin diseases. See how you translated the expression **skin diseased** in 13:44. Similarly, see how you translated the word **flowing** in 15:2.

This expression refers generally to any priest who touches something **unclean**, not to a specific priest. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a more natural expression. Alternate translation: [And any priest who touches anything unclean]

This expression uses the possessive form to describe **anything unclean** that has a human source, whether an unclean person or a discharge or blood that has come from a person. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a generic expression. Alternate translation: [anything unclean that has come from a person] or [any unclean person]
See how you translated the similar expression in 15:16.

5.note: The expression **or a person who makes him unclean** leaves out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from earlier in the sentence if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or a man who touches a person who makes him unclean] or [or a priest who touches a person who makes him unclean]

Here the word **his** refers to the unclean person whom the priest touches. If it would be helpful in your language, consider making this explicit. Alternate translation: [whatever that person’s uncleanness]
See how you handled the abstract noun **uncleanness** in 5:3.

6.note: Here the word **it** refers to any of the previously listed unclean things that a priest might touch and become unclean. If it would be helpful in your language, consider making this explicit. Alternate translation: [any of these unclean things]
Here the word **flesh** refers to a person’s body. Additionally, see how you handled the extra information in the similar expression in 1:9. Alternate translation: [he washes himself]

7.note: This is a common expression that refers to the **sun** setting at the end of the day. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when the sun sets]

The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation (with a period before): [This is because]

9.note: Here the book of Leviticus switches from describing one hypothetical priest to describing the priesthood as a whole. As such, the words **they** and **them** refer to the Israelite priests. If it would be helpful in your language, consider making this explicit. Alternate translation: [And the priests shall keep … and the priests shall not carry … they profaned it … the one making the priests holy]
See how you translated this expression in 8:35 and 18:30.

9.q: וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִשְׂא֤וּ עָלָי⁠ו֙ חֵ֔טְא וּ⁠מֵ֥תוּ ב֖⁠וֹ כִּ֣י יְחַלְּלֻ֑⁠הוּ
9.note: Here the word **it** refers to the **watch** of Yahweh, that is, Yahweh’s commands to avoid contact with unclean things while performing sacrificial duties. If it would be helpful to your readers, consider stating this plainly. Alternate translation: [and the priests shall not carry sin with regard to what I have told them to avoid and therefore die because they did what I told them to avoid, thus profaning my commands to them]

Here, **they shall not bear sin** is a common expression that refers to a priest being held responsible for their sin or wrongdoing. If that phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they shall not sin with regard to it]

The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation (with a period before): [They would die because]

10.note: Here, the expression **the holy thing** refers to any gift of food that the Israelites have sacrificed and offered to Yahweh, not to a specific food gift. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a more natural expression. Alternate translation: [any holy thing … any holy thing]

This expression uses the possessive form to describe a **dweller** (that is, a traveling guest) that is characterized by their receiving the hospitality of **the priest**. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a generic expression. Alternate translation: [A traveling guest of the priest] or [A traveler who is staying at the priest’s home]

11.note: This expression uses the possessive form to describe a slave who is **property** characterized by their having been bought by the priest’s **silver**, that is, his money. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a generic expression. Additionally, here, **silver** represents any money or currency by which a priest would purchase a slave. If it would be helpful in your language, consider stating the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he buys a person and they become his property that he purchased with his money] or [when he buys a person with his own money and they become his property]

These expressions use the words **himself** and **themselves** to emphasize how significant it was that these slaves are permitted to eat the priest’s holy food. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate this significance. Alternate translation: [even he may eat … they also may eat]

Here, the word **he** refers to the slave that the priest purchased, not to the priest. If it would be helpful for your readers, consider making this explicit. Alternate translation: [that slave may eat]

Here, the word **his** refers to a priest, while the phrase **the one born of his house** refers to a child who is born from a slave residing in the priest’s household. This expression uses the plural **they** to refer to this slave, perhaps including the mother who gave birth to him or her. If it would be helpful in your language, consider making these explicit. Alternate translation: [And a slave who is born into a priest’s household—he and his parents may eat the priest’s bread]

Here, **bread** represents the sacred portions of food that the priests received from the food gifts that the people of Israel offered to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his food]

12.note: This expression uses the word **herself** to emphasize how significant it was that the daughter of a priest is not permitted to eat her father’s holy food after her marriage. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate this significance. Alternate translation: [not even she may eat the contribution of the holy things]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **contribution**, you can express the same idea another way. Alternate translation: [the holy things that the people of Israel have contributed]

13.note: See how you handled this metaphor for descendants in 20:2. Alternate translation: [and she has no children]

Here, **bread** represents the sacred portions of food that the priests received from the food gifts that the people of Israel offered to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from her father’s food]
Alternate translation: [And no stranger may eat it]

14.note: Although the term **man** is masculine, here it is used in a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [And a person]

14.q: וְ⁠יָסַ֤ף חֲמִֽשִׁית⁠וֹ֙ עָלָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠נָתַ֥ן לַ⁠כֹּהֵ֖ן אֶת־הַ⁠קֹּֽדֶשׁ
14.note: This could mean: (1) that the person had to replace the food that he had eaten with the same kind of food or (2) that the person had to pay money to the priest for the food that he had eaten.

Here, **shall add its fifth on it** is a common expression that refers to adding one-fifth of the monetary value of a sacred food item to its total value. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then he shall take the total monetary value of the food item plus one–fifth]
The term **its fifth** refers to one part out of five equal parts.

15.note: Here, the pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Israel shall not profane … that which the people of Israel raise]
See how you translated this expression in 22:2.
See how you handled this metaphor for the people of Israel in 1:2.

Here, the word **raise** refers to the ritual gesture of lifting up an offering to Yahweh. If your language has a word for this kind of ritual gesture, consider using it here. You could also explain the significance of this action in the text or a footnote. Alternate translation: [that which they present] or [that which they offer]
Yahweh is speaking about himself in the third person. If this would not be natural in your language, you could use the first-person form. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh]

16.note: Here, **to bear the iniquity of guilt** is a common expression that refers to guilt as a physical object that needs to be carried. Because **guilt** in Leviticus can refer to both the legal status of needing to provide restitution for wrongdoing or the punishment by which restitution is provided, this expression could mean: (1) the people of Israel would become guilty and so responsible for their sin. Alternate translation: [or they shall be guilty of the sin that they committed] or (2) the word **guilt** is a metonym for punishment for the sin that they committed. Alternate translation: [or they shall receive the punishment that they deserve when they committed wrongdoing]
Alternate translation: [when they ate their holy things]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

17.q: לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר׃ דַּבֵּ֨ר אֶֽל־אַהֲרֹ֜ן וְ⁠אֶל־בָּנָ֗י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶל֙ כָּל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֑ם
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. It may be helpful to begin a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, and tell them that]

18.q: דַּבֵּ֨ר אֶֽל־אַהֲרֹ֜ן וְ⁠אֶל־בָּנָ֗י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶל֙ כָּל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֑ם
18.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing but serve different functions. While the first phrase is a command, the second phrase introduces what Moses is to say to Aaron, the priests, and the people of Israel. You can translate this parallelism into one statement that conveys this relationship. Alternate translation: [Tell Aaron and his sons and all the sons of Israel] or [Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, telling them]
See how you handled this metaphor for the people of Israel in 1:2.

This expression uses **house** to represent the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the people of Israel]
Here, the word **man** refers generally to any Israelite in general and not to men specifically. See how you handled the repetition of the word **man** in 15:2. Alternate translation: [Any person]
See how you handled these repeated words in 1:2.
Yahweh is speaking about himself in the third person. If this would not be natural in your language, you could use the first-person form. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh]

19.q: לִֽ⁠רְצֹנְ⁠כֶ֑ם תָּמִ֣ים זָכָ֔ר בַּ⁠בָּקָ֕ר בַּ⁠כְּשָׂבִ֖ים וּ⁠בָֽ⁠עִזִּֽים
19.note: This expression leaves out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words in the sentence if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for your acceptance, you shall present a perfect male among the cattle, among the sheep, or among the goats]

Here and throughout the rest of this chapter, the word “you” is plural and refers to the people of Israel as a whole and to the priests specifically. If the switch from third-person forms to second-person plural forms would not be natural in your language, consider continuing to use third-person forms. Alternate translation: [for their acceptance]

The expressions **the cattle**, **the sheep**, and **the goats** do not refer to specific groups of animals. They describe any groups of animals that an Israelite might own. Express this in the way that would be most natural in your language. Alternate translation: [among your cattle, your sheep, or your goats that you own or purchase] or, in the third person, [among any of the cattle, sheep, or goats that he owns or purchases]

20.note: Alternate translation: [Any animal on which is a blemish]

The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation (with a period before): [This is because]

21.note: Although the term **man** is masculine, here it is used in a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [And a person]
Yahweh is speaking about himself in the third person. If this would not be natural in your language, you could use the first-person form. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh]

The expressions **the cattle** and **the flock** do not refer to specific groups of animals. They describe any groups of animals that an Israelite might own. Express this in the way that would be most natural in your language. Alternate translation: [among your cattle or your flock animals that you own or purchase] or, in the third person, [among his cattle or flock animals that he owns or purchases]
Alternate translation: [No blemish shall be on it]

22.note: Yahweh is speaking about himself in the third person. If this would not be natural in your language, you could use the first-person form. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh … to me]
See how you handled the similar idiom in 4:7.

23.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not accept it]

24.q: וּ⁠מָע֤וּךְ וְ⁠כָתוּת֙ וְ⁠נָת֣וּק וְ⁠כָר֔וּת לֹ֥א תַקְרִ֖יבוּ לַֽ⁠יהוָ֑ה
24.note: The words **bruised**, **crushed**, **torn** and **cut** refer to ways in which the owner of a bovine might castrate that animal to remove its testicles. This was a common practice in the ancient world that was believed to increase the quality of the animal’s meat. Such practices are forbidden for animals that will be sacrificed as it introduces a blemish to an animal that Yahweh requires to be whole and perfect. If it would be helpful in your language, consider supplying this information in a footnote or in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [But you shall not present to Yahweh any animal whose testicles have been bruised or crushed or torn or cut] or [But you shall not present to Yahweh any animal whose owner has bruised or crushed or torn or cut the animal’s testicles]

25.q: וּ⁠מִ⁠יַּ֣ד בֶּן־נֵכָ֗ר לֹ֥א תַקְרִ֛יבוּ אֶת־לֶ֥חֶם אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠כָּל־אֵ֑לֶּה
25.note: Here the word **hand** represents the whole person. In context, this expression refers to purchasing an animal from another, specifically a **foreigner**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you shall not present the bread of your God that you acquired from the son of a foreigner]

Here, the word **son** refers generically to descendants and not just to male progeny. If your language has a generic word for children, consider using it here. Alternate translation: [a foreigner] or [someone who you consider to be a foreigner]

Here, **bread** represents food in general. Furthermore, this expression uses the possessive form to describe **bread** (that is, food) which is characterized by the fact that it is offered to **God**. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you shall not present any food as a gift to your God]

Here, the words **these** and **them** refer to the disabled or deformed animals, not to the **foreigner**. If it would be helpful in your language, consider making this explicit. Alternate translation: [from any of these blemished animals … is on these animals … is on them]

The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation (with a period before): [This is because]
Alternate translation: [their ruin is on them] or [their deformity is on them]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not accept them from you]

27.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when its mother gives birth to it]

Here, **under its mother** is a common expression that describes a young animal as being with its mother. The use of the word **under** likely describes the mother feeding the young animal. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with its mother] or [feeding from its mother]
If your language does not use this type of number, you could use a different type of number here or an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [And after seven days]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will accept it]
Yahweh is speaking about himself in the third person. If this would not be natural in your language, you could use the first-person form. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh]

28.note: Although the term **son** is masculine, here it is used in a generic sense that includes both male and female animals. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [it and its young] or [it and its offspring]

29.note: Here, **when you sacrifice a sacrifice** is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and its object that come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [And whenever you present an animal as a sacrifice of thanks]

30.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [On that day, you shall eat it] or [On that day, the people of Israel shall eat it]

31.note: Here, the words **keep** and **do** mean similar things. They both emphasize that the people must practice a habitual lifestyle of obeying God’s commands. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And you shall obey my commandments] or [And you shall keep my commandments so that you do them]

32.note: See how you translated this expression in 22:2.
Alternate translation: [but I shall be treated as holy]
See how you handled this metaphor for the people of Israel in 1:2.
